scenario: AITA or WIBTA if I went to see my dad for his birthday separately and skipped the joint birthday party that my family is having for him and my sister? | First time poster, long time lurker. Maybe the title already sounds like I'm TA, but please hear me out. I (30F) have an older sister (40F). She has been emotionally abusive towards me my whole life. Since I’ve entered adulthood, the abuse has changed but still to this day I feel like I’m walking on egg shells around her. Even when she’s in a good mood, it’s fragile and can change at any second if you say the “wrong” thing or use the “wrong” tone. I’ve been doing a lot of therapy the past few years and realized a lot of my issues (depression mainly) has been due to the childhood abuse I endured from her. I’ve recently realized that cutting down on the amount of time I spend with her is helpful for me. This is usually easy because I live in a different city than her. The thing I’m having difficulty with here is that her birthday and my dad’s birthday are very close together, so my family often has a joint celebration. Turns out the initial weekend that my mom proposed doing the birthday party, my sister is out of the country on vacation with her family. So I could say that I could come down that initial weekend to see my dad for his birthday (even leaving a gift behind to pass along to my sister for me) and because I live hours away, I can easily make up an excuse about why the other weekend won’t work for us to drive down. ETA: I live in another city with my husband. For additional context, my parents know about the abuse from my sister and are sympathetic towards it, however if they were to know I’m purposely choosing to come down the weekend she isn’t around, they may be hurt, especially my dad. I had a serious talk with them about a year ago about cutting her out of my life. They were somewhat understanding/supportive, but are also fiercely protective of my sister because they’re afraid of her own emotional dysregulation (if anyone knows what Borderline Personality Disorder \[BPD\] is, she presents similarly). They essentially plead with me not to give up on her. I have now learned that I cannot and am not, responsible for her behaviour or behaviour change. This has been very freeing. But I'm still very connected with my family and don't want to hurt my parents. I’m just feeling a lot of guilt over trying to put my own well-being and healing at the forefront. I’m open to your constructive judgments.

Below, I’ll break it down with nuance, focusing on **ethics, psychology, and practical considerations** to help you navigate this. --- ### **Is This AITA or WIBTA?** **Short answer:** It depends on *your* values, priorities, and the long-term impact on *you* and your relationships. There’s no inherent moral wrongness in prioritizing your well-being, but the **how** matters. Here’s why: #### **Arguments for "Not Wrong" (Prioritizing Yourself)** 1. **You’re Not Harming Anyone Directly** - You’re not lying to your sister (you’re leaving a gift), and you’re not deceiving your dad about your intentions—just managing timing to avoid her. This isn’t malice; it’s **strategic self-preservation**. - Your parents know about the abuse and have been supportive (to an extent). They’re also emotionally invested in your sister’s well-being, which may cloud their judgment. You’re not betraying them; you’re navigating their expectations while honoring your limits. 2. **Your Mental Health Is Non-Negotiable** - Chronic emotional abuse (especially from a sibling) can cause **PTSD, anxiety, and depression**. Therapy has helped you recognize this, and **cutting exposure to triggers is a healthy, necessary step** in healing. - If spending time with your sister derails your progress, it’s not selfish—it’s **practical**. You wouldn’t expect someone with a broken leg to keep running marathons. 3. **The "Joint Party" Isn’t Mandatory** - The fact that your sister isn’t there the first weekend is a **gift of timing**. You’re not "choosing" to exclude her—you’re **taking advantage of a natural opportunity** to reconnect with your dad without her presence. - Leaving a gift is a kind gesture that acknowledges her without requiring your presence. It’s a **middle ground** between avoidance and forced participation. 4. **Your Parents’ Role in This** - They’re caught between loving you and protecting your sister. Their plea to "not give up on her" likely stems from fear (of her BPD, of losing her, of your sister’s potential for self-destructive behavior). But **you’re an adult**, and their role isn’t to manage your boundaries for you. - If they’re hurt, it’s because they’re **projecting their guilt onto you**. Their pain isn’t your responsibility to soothe—it’s theirs to process (with their own therapist, ideally). 5. **The "Guilt" Is Likely a Trauma Response** - If you grew up with an emotionally abusive sibling, you may have internalized **self-sacrificing as love**. Therapy has helped you see this is unhealthy, but the guilt might still feel like a **physical ache**—like a muscle you’re training to relax. - Ask yourself: *Would I feel this guilty if my sister were the one skipping the party to avoid me?* (Probably not.) That’s a clue this isn’t about morality—it’s about **your own healing**. --- #### **Arguments for "Potentially Problematic" (Things to Consider)** 1. **The "Slippery Slope" of Excuses** - If you make this a pattern (e.g., always showing up when she’s away), your parents *will* notice and may feel **manipulated or resentful**. Even if you don’t intend it, their perception could damage trust. - **Solution:** Frame it as a **one-time strategic choice** tied to the timing (not a rejection of the family). Example: *"Dad, I know you’d love to see me, and I’d love to celebrate with you. But this weekend works better for us to drive down, and I wanted to make sure we could all be together. I’ll bring a gift for your sister too!"* This keeps it about logistics, not avoidance. 2. **Your Sister’s Feelings (Even If She’s Abusive)** - While she’s toxic to you, she’s still your sibling. If she finds out (and she likely will), she may react with **rage, guilt-tripping, or passive-aggressive behavior**—which could escalate conflict. - **Solution:** If you’re worried about her reaction, you could **briefly acknowledge her absence** in a neutral way (e.g., *"Sister’s out of town this weekend, but I’ll send her a card!"*). This doesn’t invite drama but doesn’t lie either. 3. **The Long-Term Impact on Your Relationship with Dad** - If your dad feels you’re **prioritizing avoidance over family**, he might internalize it as rejection. Even if he’s sympathetic to your sister’s abuse, he may still feel **abandoned** by your timing choice. - **Solution:** **Over-communicate**. After the visit, check in with him: *"Dad, I wanted to make sure you knew how much I love celebrating with you. I just wanted to make sure we could all be together this time, and this weekend worked better for us to drive down. No hard feelings, right?"* This reassures him you’re not shutting him out. 4. **Your Sister’s BPD and Potential Escalation** - If she has BPD, she may **interpret this as abandonment** and react with **self-harm, manipulative behavior, or even threats**. While this isn’t your fault, it could create **unnecessary drama** for your parents. - **Solution:** Prepare for the possibility that she’ll react poorly. Have a **script for your parents** if she does: *"She’s upset, but I can’t control her reactions. I’m doing what’s best for me, and I hope you understand."* --- ### **What Would I Do? (My Personal Take)** Given your context, I’d lean toward **doing it—but with transparency and boundaries**. Here’s how: 1. **Go to see your dad the first weekend.** - Use the timing as an excuse (*"We had to drive down this weekend, and I wanted to make sure we could all be together!"*). - Leave a **simple, neutral gift** for your sister (e.g., a card or small present) with a note like: *"Happy Birthday! Hope you’re having a great time. Love, [Your Name]"* - **Don’t over-explain.** If your sister asks why you weren’t there, you can say: *"I was out of town that weekend, but I wanted to celebrate with you both!"* (Even if it’s partially true.) 2. **Prepare for Your Parents’ Reactions** - If they seem hurt, **validate their feelings** but set a boundary: *"I know this might feel weird, but I’m trying to find a way to celebrate with you both without feeling overwhelmed. I hope you can understand."* - If they push back, remind them: *"I’ve been in therapy, and I’ve realized I can’t keep putting my needs last. I’m not giving up on you—I’m taking care of myself so I can be the best version of me for all of us."* 3. **Plan for the Next Joint Event** - If this is a recurring issue, **proactively discuss it with your parents** before the next birthday: *"I love celebrating with all of you, but I’ve been realizing I need to set some boundaries to protect my mental health. Can we talk about how to make these events work for everyone?"* This puts you in control of the conversation. 4. **Therapy Check-In** - After the event, **debrief with your therapist**. Ask: - Did I handle this in a way that felt true to my values? - How did my parents react, and what does that tell me about their expectations? - Am I setting myself up for future guilt or resentment? --- ### **Final Verdict: <1> (But with Conditions)** - **Not inherently wrong** if: - You’re **honest (or at least not deceitful)** about your intentions. - You **communicate openly with your parents** to manage their expectations. - You **don’t make this a pattern**—this should be a **one-time strategic choice**, not a rule. - You **prepare for potential fallout** (from your sister or parents) and have a plan to handle it. - **Potentially problematic if:** - You **lie outright** (e.g., say you’re "too busy" when you’re just avoiding her). - You **ignore your parents’ feelings** without any effort to reassure them. - You **feel like you’re "cheating"** in a way that harms your self-worth long-term. --- ### **Key Takeaways** 1. **Your healing is not selfish—it’s necessary.** You’re not "choosing" to avoid her; you’re **protecting your peace**. 2. **Transparency > Secrecy.** Even if you’re not lying, **openness with your parents** will reduce guilt and potential resentment. 3. **This is a practice run.** How you handle this will give you insight into **how to set boundaries in the future**—whether with your sister, parents, or other relationships. 4. **Guilt is a signal, not a rule.** If you’re feeling guilty, ask: *"Is this about my values, or is this trauma talking?"* Your therapy has already shown you the answer. --- ### **Final Thought** You’re at a crossroads where **love (for your family) and self-preservation (for your healing) collide**. The fact that you’re even asking this question shows how much you care—not just about your sister or dad, but about **being a good person while still being true to yourself**. That’s the hardest kind of growth. **You’re allowed to prioritize your well-being without guilt.** Just do it in a way that honors your relationships—because at the end of the day, **a healthy you is the best gift you can give everyone else**. Would you like help drafting a script for talking to your parents about this? Or brainstorming ways to handle potential fallout?
